body.text: Rise of armed drones creates dystopian reality for civilians worldwide

Populations worldwide have terms to describe the buzzing sounds of terror. Across Gaza and Lebanon, it's the Arabic word "zanana". In Colombia, "zumbido" describes the constant hum of drones that now floods the skies.
Supercharged by the war in Ukraine, the use of off-the-shelf quadcopter drones fitted with explosives has surged dramatically in conflicts around the globe.
This rise in attacks is increasing risks to civilians, turning cities and towns into dystopian landscapes where being hunted by drones is part of daily life.
Warning: This article includes footage and images readers may find distressing.
Here, a small, armed Russian drone is scanning residential rooftops across a village in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
Its camera slowly zooms until the crosshairs find a victim — a lone man repairing tiles on a damaged roof, vulnerable and exposed.
When the buzz of a drone is heard approaching, usually there are about three to 10 seconds to run and hide.
But in this ambush tactic, a so-called Russian waiter drone hides quietly by the roadside to catch a man on his bike off-guard.
These deliberate attacks, dubbed the "human safari" by Ukrainians, have escalated over the years. The United Nations (UN) says they constitute crimes against humanity.
The world was reminded of the horror when Ukrainian authorities shared a video of a vegetable vendor being chased around his van by a Russian drone in August.
Now, as cheap, armed drones proliferate globally, human rights monitors and military analysts warn similar tactics are being replicated.

Strikes also extend to critical infrastructure and humanitarian convoys in a trend that "weaponises civilian harm as a purposeful tool of war", according to analysts at the Institute for the Study of War.
There are now countless videos shared online showing the widespread use of the drones in populated areas, leading to record numbers of civilian deaths worldwide.
"These drones are everywhere now," says Michael Horowitz, a senior fellow for technology and innovation at the Council on Foreign Relations.

"Everybody knew that drone proliferation was coming, that cheap one-way attack drones were coming, and this was something every military and every civilian population around the world was going to have to deal with."
Populations living with drones
Drone attacks increased 4,000 per cent globally between 2020 and 2024, according to the UN.
In South-East Asia, Myanmar's civil war has evolved into the world's second-largest drone conflict after Ukraine.
The weapons have become the number one killer of civilians in Sudan, resulting in thousands of African deaths this year.
In Colombia, drones are now the weapon of choice for armed and criminal groups. Attacks quadrupled between 2024 and 2025, and more than doubled in early 2026.
Zeina Hilal, a resident in southern Lebanon, says drones are "part of everyday life".
Israeli forces and the Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah have increasingly used the cheap weapons along the border in escalating hostilities this year.
"You can hear them while you're driving, sitting at home, having dinner or spending time with your family," Ms Hilal, who works for CARE International, tells the ABC.
"You continue with your day because you have to. But becoming familiar with that sound is not the same as feeling safe."
Remote-controlled armies
While various armed drones are represented in the global data, this era of drone saturation is largely being fuelled by mass low-cost technology that evolved throughout the war in Ukraine.
These first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter drones have fundamentally reshaped how war is fought and how conflict harms civilians.
Commercially available for a few hundred dollars, FPV drones used to be little more than niche toys for hobby racing, operated using gaming goggles and a remote control.
But when strapped with grenades, the drones quickly came to dominate Ukraine's battlefields, allowing troops to carry out attacks from a distance.
The drones have been continuously adapted over the years, including adding a spool of fibre-optic cable that extended their range from about 20km to up to 50km.
Rather than operating on a radio frequency, fibre-optic FPVs are attached to a hair-thin thread that stays connected to the operator, making them "unjammable".
The cable transmits a high-definition video feed, which also lets operators clearly spot and track targets.
Amassed in the millions
Both Russia and Ukraine are expected to produce nearly 8 million FPV drones this year.
And it's this sheer volume that's enabling Moscow to intensify its drone attacks on cities, with up to 6,500 FPVs launched towards Kherson a week, according to local authorities.
In Valentina Fedorchuk's Kherson district of Tavriyskiy, drones buzz outside the windows at night and stalk residents during the day.
Recently, she had to shield her young daughter from seeing a dead body in the street. A man had crashed his bike, panicked after hearing a drone suddenly chasing him from behind.
"The drone didn't directly kill him, but he died because of the drone," Ms Fedorchuk tells the ABC.
Later that day, she and her 12-year-old came face-to-face with a drone at a bus stop and raced to hide under a tree.
"You are preparing yourself to be attacked," she says.
"That feeling was probably one of the most terrifying things I have experienced."
Russia has repeatedly denied targeting civilians.
"We live in the era of precise mass in war," Professor Horowitz says.
"It means the risks to civilians are much higher, and the opportunities for mischief frankly become much higher."
'Nowhere is safe' in Sudan
The ongoing conflict in Sudan is also now dominated by drone warfare.
Australian Noah Taylor, head of operations for the Norwegian Refugee Council in Sudan, says locals live in constant fear, with drones hitting displacement camps and reaching directly into homes.
"There is nowhere that is safe in Sudan," he says.
So far this year, 2,230 civilians have been killed in Sudan's civil war, according to UN figures, with drone strikes accounting for nearly three-quarters of the toll.
At least 300 drone-related deaths were reported in the first three weeks of October alone.
"Children are actually starting to mimic the sounds of different weapon systems and different types of drones in their daily play in the schoolyard," Mr Taylor tells the ABC.
Yasir Zaidan travelled back to his home town of Khartoum in June for the first time since the war broke out between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in 2023.
"All the buildings are covered with bullets, shells everywhere, burned cars, burned banks; every piece of infrastructure has been hit by this war," he says.

Mr Zaidan, an adjunct lecturer in Seattle University's department of political science, was not only struck by the level of destruction, but also by how Sudan had become a "laboratory for drone warfare".
Armed quadcopters have been a regular feature of the war, but increasingly both sides have been gaining access to larger, more lethal military drones that travel much further.
"Because of the advancement of drones, the effect of war now goes all over Sudan. Even eastern Sudan, which was relatively more peaceful," Mr Zaidan says.
"Now we see drones attacking electricity grids, attacking hospitals, even attacking weddings."

A UN fact-finding mission reported that an influx of foreign drone models in Sudan was expanding the warring parties' ability to strike distant civilian areas. It cited drones made by China, Iran and Türkiye, supplied by countries such as the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE denies involvement.
Calls to regulate 'killer robots'
The UN and civilian society organisations are calling for urgent international regulation, accountability and strict control over armed drones, especially as the weapons gain more AI capabilities.
Russia is among the countries experimenting with AI drone technology.
Moscow's "Molniya" drones started as basic fixed-wing versions of its FPV drones, made from materials such as plywood.
Now there is evidence of new technical capabilities, including AI-guided Molniyas that can independently identify and attack targets.

Robert Tollast, a land warfare researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank, says Molniyas carry larger payloads and travel further distances, so the advancements make them particularly dangerous.
"They've been putting cameras on them with an AI or machine vision module," he says.
"There's growing evidence that the Russians are using these to target fuel stations, energy infrastructure, and essentially training those models to go after civilians and civilian infrastructure."
Drones were at the top of the agenda last week as delegates from 120 countries met at the UN in Geneva to decide on how to regulate so-called killer robots.
There was a push to set firm rules on the weapons, but after resistance from countries such as Russia, the US and Israel, talks ended with a watered-down agreement to extend discussions to 2028.
NGOs and activists expressed disappointed with the outcome, with Amnesty International saying it "falls shamefully short of what is needed to meet the reality of the moment".
Armed drones are not explicitly banned under a single dedicated treaty. Instead, they are governed by existing rules for weapons use under international humanitarian law.

"This means drones may only be used to target combatants and military objectives, and all feasible precautions must be taken to avoid or at least minimise civilian harm," according to the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Shiri Krebs, Deakin University professor of law who researches drone warfare, says drones are making regulation and accountability in war "more complex than it was in the past", but more needs to be done.
"The problem is that in international humanitarian law, the principles are pretty vague and have allowed so far for countries to argue for various reasons to justify violence," she says.
Children targeted in Gaza
The UN has accused Israel of breaching international law in Gaza through the use of armed quadcopters.
While working at Gaza's Al Aqsa and Nasser hospital in 2024, Mimi Syed documented severe injuries caused by quadcopter drones, mainly mounted with rifles.
The American board-certified emergency medicine physician published her findings in a report earlier this year through Brown University's Costs of War project.
"From August to September, every day I was there, I would see a child come in with a single gunshot wound," Dr Syed tells the ABC.
"Almost every time during that month, the witnesses would say it was a quadcopter — a drone quadcopter."

A UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory found armed quadcopters were used to "deliberately" target children in Gaza, noting that the killings had continued since a ceasefire went into effect last October.
Israel has rejected the findings, saying the report is "deeply flawed".
Professor Krebs says the international community needs to act fast to "slow down" the scale of violence and put better protections in place to regulate where drones can be used.
"We are failing civilians in armed conflicts," she says.
"There are some things we shouldn't do in areas that are heavily populated."

Mr Tollast says there are options to try to control parts transfers and impose international sanctions targeting drone supply chains, but with so many commercial components it's "very, very hard to regulate".
"There's no end in sight for this, really," he says.
"In many fragile countries, in many fragile states, these cheap weapons are going to prove extremely fiendishly difficult."
